The Mystery of the White Lady

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
.....the age old mystery of the White Lady of the Brandberg possible solved.

Unique Selling Point:
It is a multi-layered story and deals with history archaeology and rock art in Namibia. It can visually be very strong and it is an unusual story -- we seldom get the opportunity to do this kind of story. It is also new research.

Summary:
In Namibia, an age-old mystery was painted on rocks in a remote part of the country. It is known as the White Lady of the Brandberg. It is a depiction of a white woman in rock art that seems out of place: when the painting was done there were no white people South of the Equator. So people believed it was a local Shaman, painted white. Now research done by prominent Namibian architect and artist Linus Malherbe indicated that it could be a white woman of Viking origin. An astounding theory. -- hould not be there.

Further information:
In Namibia, an age-old mystery was painted on rocks in a remote part of the country. It is known as the White Lady of the Brandberg. It is a depiction of a white woman in rock art that should not be there. Over the years many theories have been postulated for this anomaly. Some suggested Phoenician influences and in the latter part of the 20th century, African origin narratives were becoming more prevalent. In 2020 a new theory emerged. It is from well-known Namibian architect and writer, Linus Malherbe. He debunks existing hypotheses and claims that the white lady is actually a Viking woman from lost explorers who left their mark in northern-western Namibia. He illustrates that especially Himba culture and traditions were influenced by these visitors from more than a millennium ago. And it is much more than just a theory – he backs it up with wide research into Mediterranean culture and art and comparing that to what is found in the rock art of the Brandberg. He also looks at aspects of architecture and traditions amongst the Himba or the area.

The theory is that the art depicts a group of Iberian Viking, Moorish and Nigerian explorers looking for Garnets, Obsidian, Tourmline and other gemstones in the Tisisab Valley. Clothing, weapons (bow type, stringing, iron arrowhead, hunting knives), hair, armour, decorations, foreign flower and seem to be very close to what we know of the Vikings.


Interviewees:

• Linus Malherbe (based in Namibia)
He is one of Namibia’s most prominent and prolific artists with a huge interest in Namibian art history. He has been studying the White Lady intensely for many years and has come up with an astounding theory about the origin of the painting.

• John Kinahan (based in JHB)
He is the Honorary Curator of Archaeology at the National Museum of Namibia, and Honorary Research Fellow at the School of Geography, Archaeology and Environmental Sciences, University of the Witwatersrand, South Africa. He is currently co-Principal Investigator for a National Science Foundation research project based at Arizona State University on the use of strontium isotopes as a means to investigate archaeological evidence of regional trade networks in the Namib Desert. He has written several books on the archaeology of the Namib desert.

• Dr. Mark Callaghan
He holds a Ph.D. from the University of Oxford and is an Art Historian and Historian who specializes in the Viking era.

The interviews will be done by Zoom.

We will hire a cameraman in Namibia to shoot our interviewees there and to go to the Barndberg to shoot on location there.

We will attempt to get permission to shoot some links in the the Rock Art Museum at Wits.


Extra Budget Items:
Shooting in Namibia
Car rental 1.5 days
Fuel
Accommodation for 1 night
S&T 1.5 days

Script:


V/O:
This is the Brandberg mountain range. It is located in one of the most inhospitable places on earth -- the Namib desert. It is also known as the Dwaures Mountain. This mountain range is a dome shaped granite intrusion that rises high above the surrounding desert.

It has water and shelter and over thousands of years, it has provided refuge to generations nomadic hunter gatherers. These people, the ancestors of today’s San, left their mark on the rock overhangs and the mountain is home to at least 45 000 individual rock art paintings.
LINK:
Among the thousands of rock art friezes one group of figures stand out, and it also caught the eye of early European explorers.
V/O:
This frieze is painted on a rock overhang, located deep in the mountain, along this dry Tsisab river ravine.

In the frieze an exquisite central figure dominates. This image has become THE iconic rock art painting in Southern Africa. It is known as the White Lady of the Brandberg, and since Europeans first set eyes on it, is has been shrouded in mystery and controversy.

The controversy was started by the first European explorer who stumbled across it in 1917. He said, “the Egyptian-Mediterranean style of all the figures is surprising".

Dr Sam Challis is the head of the Rock Art Research Institute at Wits and says the idea that Europeans created the art, attracted a lot of attention in Europe.
Sam:
By the end of the second world war the very famous and eminent pre-historian Abbe Henri Breuil who had become famous in Europe for having covered the discovery of Lasco, the very famous Ice Age painting in France, came to this part of the world and it was he who was responsible for calling it the so-called White Lady.
V/O:
Breuill was influential and the idea that there was an image the image of a white woman in ancient rock art in Southern Africa, spread like wildfire.
LINK:
And so the painting became known as the White lady and people from all over the world came just to see it.
V/O:
However, Challis says Breuil’s thesis was soon challenged by those who studied rock art and indigenous cultures.

Dr John Kinnahan is an eminent Namibian archaeologist.
John:
There was a huge argument about it, but it was very quickly resolved that there was no basis for that idea at all.
V/O:
Instead, scholarly consensus was reached that what is depicted on the rock overhang is not a white female, but an indigenous male medicine man or Shaman. And to this day guides like John Thaniseb, who took us to the famous rock-overhang, explain this to visitors.
John:
As you can see, only men carry bow and arrow, not lady. He carries a bow and arrow and he carries a stick… when the Shaman… they use a stick with medicine inside.
V/O:
The Wildbeest Kuil Rock Art Centre near Kimberley is a community-based rock art project on land owned by the kung en kwe San. It is perspective provided by indigenous or local experts like Petrus Wilson that can help to establish the white lady’s ultimate meaning.
Petrus:
Ek dink dit is ‘n goeie ding as indigenous mense betrokke is wanneer hierdie navorsing gedoen word. So ja, ‘n mens kan nie rotskuns net op enige manier interpreteer nie.
V/O:
The idea that the White Lady is a male Shaman went unchallenged for many decades……... until recently.
LINK:
Now an artist’s analysis of the image suggests that the image is indeed female, and actually the depiction of a Viking woman who visited Namibia about a thousand years ago.
V/O:
This idea was proposed by prominent Namibian architect and artist, Linus Malhebe who carefully studied the detail of the frieze. He also put the theory forward in a lecture at the Namibian Scientific Society and published it in a recent book.
LINUS:
She to me, is Medieval, from European descent, and definitely female.
V/O:
Malherbe bases his theory mostly on the notes and this sketch made by Breuill, and a 1945 photograph. He says she is female because she lacks a penis while all the male figures in the frieze have clearly defined ones, and the figure also wears a barbette, or Medieval chin strap that only women wore.

Malherbe further says that the figure’s face is a European face and has long red hair. The figure is also wearing shoes, which is very unusual.
Malherbe:
she is not a bushman medicine man or Shaman.
V/O:
Malherbe has also created a large artwork in which he depicts the White Lady as a White Medieval Female Warrior of Viking descent who came down the coast of Africa to Namibia with a group to engage in gemstone trading.

He says the painting was done by this group, and elements in it fit perfectly with the Medieval period, SUCH AS :
• The central figure carries a European style, asymmetrical recurve bow and she has archer’s cuffs.
• The metal tip of the arrow is unusual for Africa.
• She also wears a wide leather belt and leather armour over a medieval gambeson.
• He further says the figure is wearing chausses, or leggings, something which Breuill also referred to in his notes.
Linus:
And he described it in detail, the red strappings at the top and how it was fastened.
V/O:
Malherbe says in general his work has been well received so far but realizes that it flies in the face of current scholarship on the interpretation of rock art.

However, his ideas have also attracted overseas attention, says UK based historian and art historian Mark Callahan who specializes in the Viking era.
Mark:
I think with Malherbe’s hypothesis, I think is deserves some respect actually. It is intriguing and at times compelling. So his visual analysis of some of the items in the frieze in the rock painting is very intriguing. So, we have the thick wide Viking belt, we have the asymmetrical bow, we have the Viking style shoulder strap. These are all indicative of Viking culture. So, I certainly do not think it should be dismissed.
V/O:
However, Callahan also points out that the painting has not been dated yet – so, it can be from the medieval period or date back many thousands of years.

There is also no archaeological evidence of Vikings travelling further down the coast of Africa than Morocco.

And Callaghan adds that there is no evidence that Vikings ever traded in sub-Saharan gemstones. This, he says, makes many scholars hesitant to fully support Malherbe.
Mark:
So, no one dismisses the possibility. They recognize that there is a distinct possibility and that there seems to be some evidence that points to his conclusions, but no one can really commit to it being anything more than a possibility. The evidence is simply not strong enough to be certain and put their names to it, for instance.
V/O:
However, local rock art researhcers and archaeologists find Malherbe’s revival of an old controversial theory deeply flawed.
Sam:
Yes, the White Lady is a myth. It is a story that was cooked up by people to suit their agendas in various periods of time.
V/O:
And he says it goes back to pre- conceptions that were prevalent when Europeans first lay eyes on the paintings.
Sam:
The thinking in those days was that because these images are so incredibly beautiful, they could not have been made by simple people like the San.
V/O:
Furthermore, Challis says Breuill deliberately altered his sketch to make the figure appear female and excluded a penis. A detailed copy of the painting made from a photograph in the 1970’s, clearly shows a decorated penis, drawn in much the same way as that of another male figure in the frieze. The face also differs markedly from Breuill’s sketch.

Further, Challis says scholars agree that rock art cannot be interpreted in any arbitrary manner.
John:
And the rock art is the expression of the intensified religious and ritual life.
Challis:
It is not just a record of events. There people are not like you and I, they did not just write diaries on the rock face nor are the images of the antelope some sort of menu that they would like eat or aspire to have for their lunch, or simplistic things like that. My colleagues and I would say that you have to come at it from a San perspective, or as close to San perspective that can be managed. And it transpires that these are clearly visions of the spirit world.

And it is much more than just a theory – he backs it up with wide research into Mediterranean culture and art and comparing that to what is found in the rock art of the Brandberg. He also looks at aspects of architecture and traditions amongst the Himba or the area. The theory is that the art depicts a group of Iberian Viking, Moorish and Nigerian explorers looking for Garnets, Obsidian, Tourmline and other gemstones in the Tisisab Valley. Clothing, weapons (bow type, stringing, iron arrowhead, hunting knives), hair, armour, decorations, foreign flower and seem to be very close to what we know of the Vikings. Interviewees: • Linus Malherbe (based in Namibia) He is one of Namibia’s most prominent and prolific artists with a huge interest in Namibian art history. He has been studying the White Lady intensely for many years and has come up with an astounding theory about the origin of the painting. • John Kinahan (based in JHB) He is the Honorary Curator of Archaeology at the National Museum of Namibia, and Honorary Research Fellow at the School of Geography, Archaeology and Environmental Sciences, University of the Witwatersrand, South Africa. He is currently co-Principal Investigator for a National Science Foundation research project based at Arizona State University on the use of strontium isotopes as a means to investigate archaeological evidence of regional trade networks in the Namib Desert. He has written several books on the archaeology of the Namib desert. • Dr. Mark Callaghan He holds a Ph.D. from the University of Oxford and is an Art Historian and Historian who specializes in the Viking era. The interviews will be done by Zoom. We will hire a cameraman in Namibia to shoot our interviewees there and to go to the Barndberg to shoot on location there. We will attempt to get permission to shoot some links in the the Rock Art Museum at Wits.
